Answer ALL questions: Section A is Pure Mathematics (questions 1 to 35) and Section B is Statistics (questions 36 to 50). Formulae booklets and calculators are allowed. Each question has FOUR suggested answers A, B, C and D; mark only one answer for each question (if you mark more than one answer you score zero for that question). Avoid spending too much time on any one question. Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room. The scan is complete: cover page and the five pages of questions (pages 2 to 6).

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION A: PURE MATHEMATICS**

Given that $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, where $f(x)=\dfrac{x+2}{x+1}$, the range of $f$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Write $y=\dfrac{x+2}{x+1}=1+\dfrac{1}{x+1}$. Since $\dfrac{1}{x+1}$ can take every real value except $0$, $y$ takes every real value except $1$. Equivalently, solving $y(x+1)=x+2$ for $x$ gives $x=\dfrac{2-y}{y-1}$, which exists only when $y\ne1$. So the range is all real numbers except $1$ (the options use the dummy variable $x$, but only the excluded value matters). Option C, $x\ne-1$, is the DOMAIN restriction (the denominator vanishes), not the range; option B uses the zero of the numerator. (Strictly, $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is not defined at $x=-1$; the question intends the natural domain $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{-1\}$.) **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If functions $g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ and $h:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ are such that $g(x)=3x-2$ and $h(x)=x-1$, then $(g\circ h)(x)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: $(g\circ h)(x)=g\big(h(x)\big)=g(x-1)=3(x-1)-2=3x-3-2=3x-5$. The common slip is to compose in the wrong order: $(h\circ g)(x)=h(3x-2)=3x-3$, which is option B. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\4&5&6\\7&8&9\end{pmatrix}$, then the cofactor of the element $6$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The element $6$ is in row $2$, column $3$. Its minor $M_{23}$ is the determinant left after deleting row $2$ and column $3$: $\begin{vmatrix}1&2\\7&8\end{vmatrix}$. The cofactor is $C_{23}=(-1)^{2+3}M_{23}=-\begin{vmatrix}1&2\\7&8\end{vmatrix}$ (its value is $-(8-14)=6$). Option A is the minor without the sign $(-1)^{i+j}$; options C and D wrongly multiply by the element itself. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $\dfrac{2x+1}{(1-x)(2+x)}\equiv\dfrac{A}{1-x}+\dfrac{B}{2+x}$, then
questions.corrige_markdown: Multiply through by $(1-x)(2+x)$: $2x+1\equiv A(2+x)+B(1-x)$. Put $x=1$: $3=3A$, so $A=1$. Put $x=-2$: $-3=3B$, so $B=-1$. Check at $x=0$: $2A+B=2-1=1$, equal to $2(0)+1=1$. The other options come from a sign slip on the factor $1-x$ (it is $1-x$, not $x-1$). **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The normal vector to the plane $6x+2y-7z-12=0$ is

*Options as printed:* A) $-6\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}+7\mathbf{k}$   B) $6\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}-12\mathbf{k}$   C) $6\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}-12\mathbf{k}$   D) $6\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}-7\mathbf{k}$
questions.corrige_markdown:
A plane $ax+by+cz=d$ has normal vector $\mathbf{n}=a\mathbf{i}+b\mathbf{j}+c\mathbf{k}$, the vector of the coefficients of $x$, $y$, $z$. Here $\mathbf{n}=6\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}-7\mathbf{k}$ (option D); the constant term $-12$ does not enter (options B and C wrongly use it). Note that option A is $-\mathbf{n}$, which is parallel to $\mathbf{n}$ and therefore ALSO perpendicular to the plane: the question does not say which of the two opposite normals is wanted. Option D is the standard textbook normal, the one intended by the key.

**Intended answer: D ($6\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}-7\mathbf{k}$).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are roots of a quadratic equation such that $\alpha+\beta=3$ and $\alpha\beta=\dfrac32$. The value of $\alpha^2+\beta^2$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: $\alpha^2+\beta^2=(\alpha+\beta)^2-2\alpha\beta=3^2-2\cdot\dfrac32=9-3=6$. Option D, $9$, is $(\alpha+\beta)^2$ with the term $-2\alpha\beta$ forgotten. (The equation is $2x^2-6x+3=0$, with discriminant $36-24=12>0$, so the roots are real.) **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: When $f(x)=2x^3+x^2-13x+6$ is divided by $(x+1)$ the remainder is
questions.corrige_markdown: By the remainder theorem the remainder on division by $(x+1)=(x-(-1))$ is $f(-1)=2(-1)^3+(-1)^2-13(-1)+6=-2+1+13+6=18$. Option B, $-4$, is $f(1)$ (the remainder on dividing by $x-1$), and D, $-6$, is $f(0)$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The range of values of $x$ for which $|x+4|\le2$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: $|x+4|\le2\iff-2\le x+4\le2\iff-6\le x\le-2$. Option B describes the opposite inequality $|x+4|\ge2$ (the region outside the interval), and A and C keep only one of the two bounds. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $\sin\theta=\dfrac45$ and $\theta$ is an acute angle, then the exact value of $2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: For an acute angle $\cos\theta=\sqrt{1-\sin^2\theta}=\sqrt{1-\dfrac{16}{25}}=\dfrac35$ (the $3$-$4$-$5$ triangle). Then $2\sin\theta\cos\theta=2\cdot\dfrac45\cdot\dfrac35=\dfrac{24}{25}$, that is $\sin2\theta$. Option D, $\dfrac{12}{25}$, forgets the factor $2$; B and C are $\sin^2\theta$ and $\cos^2\theta$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The values of $x$ that satisfy the equation $3^{2x}-10\left(3^{x+1}\right)+9=0$ are

*Options as printed:* A) $x=1,\ x=9$   B) $x=-2,\ x=0$   C) $x=-1,\ x=-9$   D) $x=0,\ x=2$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $u=3^x>0$, so that $3^{2x}=u^2$ and $3^{x+1}=3u$.

**As printed**, $3^{2x}-10\left(3^{x+1}\right)+9=0$ becomes $u^2-30u+9=0$, so $u=15\pm6\sqrt6$ (both positive) and $x=\log_3\left(15\pm6\sqrt6\right)\approx3.087$ or $-1.087$. None of these values is in the list of options (substituting $x=1,9,-2,0,-1,-9,2$ never gives $0$).

**Probable intended equation**: $3^{2x}-10\left(3^{x}\right)+9=0$ (exponent $x$, not $x+1$). Then $u^2-10u+9=0$, so $(u-1)(u-9)=0$, $u=1$ or $u=9$, hence $3^x=1$ gives $x=0$ and $3^x=9$ gives $x=2$. Check: $x=0$: $1-10+9=0$; $x=2$: $81-90+9=0$. This is option D.

The printed exponent and the options are inconsistent, which is why the question is left open: the intended answer is D only under the corrected equation.

**Intended answer: D ($x=0,\ x=2$).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: If $y=0$ when $x=2$, then the solution of the differential equation $y\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Separate the variables: $\int y\,dy=\int x\,dx$, so $\dfrac{y^2}{2}=\dfrac{x^2}{2}+c$, i.e. $y^2=x^2+C$ with $C=2c$. When $x=2$, $y=0$: $0=4+C$, so $C=-4$ and $y^2=x^2-4$. Using $c=-2$ directly in $y^2=x^2+c$ (forgetting to double the constant) leads to option C. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: On the set $A=\{2,4,8,16,\ \}$ [the scan shows a blank after $16$; read as the set continuing in the same pattern], a relation $R$ is defined by $x\,R\,y$ if and only if $y$ is a multiple of $x$. $R$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: Test the three properties. REFLEXIVE: every $x$ is a multiple of itself ($x=1\cdot x$), so $xRx$ holds: D is false. SYMMETRIC: $2R4$ ($4$ is a multiple of $2$) but $4R2$ is false ($2$ is not a multiple of $4$): B is false. TRANSITIVE: if $y=kx$ and $z=my$ for integers $k,m$ then $z=(km)x$ is a multiple of $x$, so $xRy$ and $yRz$ give $xRz$: R is transitive. Since R is not symmetric it is not an equivalence relation (A is false); it is in fact a partial order (reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The line segment $AB$, where $A(5,5)$ and $B(3,-2)$ is the diameter of a circle. The equation of the circle is
questions.corrige_markdown: For a circle with diameter endpoints $(x_1,y_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2)$ the equation is $(x-x_1)(x-x_2)+(y-y_1)(y-y_2)=0$ (the angle in a semicircle is a right angle, so $\overrightarrow{PA}\cdot\overrightarrow{PB}=0$ for every point $P$ of the circle). With $A(5,5)$, $B(3,-2)$: $(x-5)(x-3)+(y-5)(y+2)=0$. Check: both $A$ and $B$ satisfy it. The other options change the sign of one coordinate of $A$ or $B$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are given as $\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{b}=2\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k}$. The vector product $\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: $\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}&\mathbf{j}&\mathbf{k}\\1&3&2\\2&-1&2\end{vmatrix}=\mathbf{i}(3\cdot2-2\cdot(-1))-\mathbf{j}(1\cdot2-2\cdot2)+\mathbf{k}(1\cdot(-1)-3\cdot2)=8\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}-7\mathbf{k}$. The $\mathbf{j}$ component is $-(2-4)=+2$: forgetting the minus sign in front of the $\mathbf{j}$ term gives $-2$ (options B and C). Check: the result is perpendicular to $\mathbf{a}$ ($8+6-14=0$) and to $\mathbf{b}$ ($16-2-14=0$). **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The volume generated when the area of the finite region enclosed by the $x$-axis and the curve $y=2x^2-4x$ is rotated completely about the $x$-axis is
questions.corrige_markdown: The curve meets the $x$-axis where $2x^2-4x=2x(x-2)=0$, i.e. at $x=0$ and $x=2$: these are the limits of the finite region. Rotating about the $x$-axis, $V=\pi\int_a^b y^2\,dx=\pi\int_0^2(2x^2-4x)^2\,dx$ (the region lies below the axis between $0$ and $2$, but squaring removes the sign; $V=\dfrac{64\pi}{15}$). Options A, C, D use the wrong limits ($-2$ is not a root) and, for C and D, a factor $2\pi$ that does not belong to a rotation about the $x$-axis. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A root of the equation $x^3+x-26=0$, lies between
questions.corrige_markdown: Let $f(x)=x^3+x-26$, which is continuous. $f(1)=-24$, $f(2)=8+2-26=-16$, $f(3)=27+3-26=4$, $f(4)=42$. $f$ changes sign between $x=2$ ($f<0$) and $x=3$ ($f>0$), so by the intermediate value theorem a root lies in $(2,3)$ (it is about $2.85$). $f$ is strictly increasing, so this is the only real root and the other intervals contain none. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The sum of the first $n$ terms of a sequence is given by $S_n=2n^2+n$. The $n^{\text{th}}$ term of this sequence is
questions.corrige_markdown: For $n\ge2$, $u_n=S_n-S_{n-1}=(2n^2+n)-\big(2(n-1)^2+(n-1)\big)=2n^2+n-2n^2+4n-2-n+1=4n-1$. For $n=1$, $u_1=S_1=3=4(1)-1$, so the formula holds for all $n\ge1$. Check: $u_2=S_2-S_1=10-3=7=4(2)-1$. Option D, $4n+3$, is $S_{n+1}-S_n=u_{n+1}$ (an index shift). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The first three terms in the binomial expansion of $(1+3x)^{-1}$ are

*Options as printed:* A) $1-3x+9x^2$   B) $1+3x-9x^2$   C) $1-3x-9x^2$   D) $1-3x+9x^2$
questions.corrige_markdown:
For $|x|<\tfrac13$: $(1+3x)^{-1}=1+(-1)(3x)+\dfrac{(-1)(-2)}{2!}(3x)^2+\cdots=1-3x+9x^2-\cdots$.

Check with the geometric series $\dfrac1{1+r}=1-r+r^2-\cdots$ where $r=3x$. So the correct expansion is $1-3x+9x^2$. Options B and C have wrong signs.

Defect of the printed question: options A and D are printed identically ($1-3x+9x^2$), so two options are correct at once. The question is therefore left open.

**Answer: A (and D, which is identical).**

**Intended answer: A ($1-3x+9x^2$).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The value of $x$ for which $\log2+\log(2x+5)=1$ is

*Options as printed:* A) $2$   B) $-\dfrac12$   C) $\dfrac12$   D) $-2$
questions.corrige_markdown:
**With common logarithms (base 10)**, as the notation $\log$ normally means: $\log2+\log(2x+5)=\log\left[2(2x+5)\right]=1$ gives $2(2x+5)=10$, so $2x+5=5$ and $x=0$. The condition $2x+5>0$ holds. The value $x=0$ is not among the options. (With natural logarithms the equation gives $x=\dfrac{e-10}{4}\approx-1.82$, not an option either.)

**With logarithms to base 2** (where $\log_22=1$): $\log_22+\log_2(2x+5)=1$ gives $\log_2(2x+5)=0$, so $2x+5=1$ and $x=-2$. Check: $\log_22+\log_21=1+0=1$. This is option D, the only option for which the equation holds in some standard reading.

The base of the logarithm is not printed, and the base-10 reading has no correct option, so the question cannot be marked automatically: it is left open. The most likely intended answer is D (base 2).

**Intended answer: D ($-2$).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to2}\left(\dfrac{x-2}{x^2-5x+6}\right)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Factorise: $x^2-5x+6=(x-2)(x-3)$. For $x\ne2$, $\dfrac{x-2}{(x-2)(x-3)}=\dfrac1{x-3}$, and the limit as $x\to2$ is $\dfrac1{2-3}=-1$. The direct substitution gives $\dfrac00$, an indeterminate form, so neither option A (numerator tends to $0$) nor option C (denominator tends to $0$) can be concluded from it. Option D has the sign of $x-3$ wrong. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\int_0^1\dfrac{x}{1+x^2}\,dx=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Since $\dfrac{d}{dx}(1+x^2)=2x$, $\int\dfrac{x}{1+x^2}dx=\dfrac12\ln(1+x^2)+c$. Hence $\int_0^1=\dfrac12\ln2-\dfrac12\ln1=\dfrac12\ln2\approx0.347$. Option A drops the factor $\dfrac12$ (it is also numerically equal to option D, $\dfrac12\ln4=\ln2$, which is just as wrong). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $y^3=12x-x^3$, then $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=$
questions.corrige_markdown: Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$: $3y^2\dfrac{dy}{dx}=12-3x^2$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{12-3x^2}{3y^2}=\dfrac{4-x^2}{y^2}$. Option A has the opposite sign; B and C come from a sign error on the derivative of $-x^3$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The complex number $z=\dfrac{1+2i}{3-4i}$ can be expressed in the form $a+bi$ as
questions.corrige_markdown: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate $3+4i$: $z=\dfrac{(1+2i)(3+4i)}{(3-4i)(3+4i)}=\dfrac{3+4i+6i+8i^2}{9+16}=\dfrac{3-8+10i}{25}=\dfrac{-5+10i}{25}=-\dfrac15+\dfrac25 i$. Using $i^2=+1$ instead of $-1$ would give $\dfrac{11}{25}+\dfrac25 i$ (option A); option C has the wrong sign on the imaginary part. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The argument of the complex number $z=\dfrac{1+i\sqrt3}{1+i}$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: $\arg(1+i\sqrt3)=\dfrac\pi3$ and $\arg(1+i)=\dfrac\pi4$. For a quotient, $\arg z=\arg(1+i\sqrt3)-\arg(1+i)=\dfrac\pi3-\dfrac\pi4=\dfrac{\pi}{12}$. Check by rationalising: $z=\dfrac{(1+i\sqrt3)(1-i)}{2}=\dfrac{(1+\sqrt3)+i(\sqrt3-1)}{2}$, with positive real and imaginary parts and $\tan\arg z=\dfrac{\sqrt3-1}{\sqrt3+1}=2-\sqrt3=\tan15^\circ$. Option C is the sum $\dfrac\pi3+\dfrac\pi4$, and D is the difference taken in the wrong order. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The general solution of the equation $\sin\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The general solution of $\sin\theta=\sin\alpha$ is $\theta=n\pi+(-1)^n\alpha$, $n\in\mathbb{Z}$. Here $\sin\alpha=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ gives $\alpha=\dfrac\pi3$. So $\theta=n\pi+(-1)^n\dfrac\pi3$. Check: $n=0$ gives $\dfrac\pi3$; $n=1$ gives $\pi-\dfrac\pi3=\dfrac{2\pi}3$, both with sine $\dfrac{\sqrt3}2$. Options B and D use $\dfrac\pi6$ (the angle whose sine is $\dfrac12$), and A has the wrong sign. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The tangent of the acute angle between the lines $y=5x-7$ and $y=x-6$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The gradients are $m_1=5$ and $m_2=1$. The angle $\phi$ between the lines satisfies $\tan\phi=\left|\dfrac{m_1-m_2}{1+m_1m_2}\right|=\dfrac{4}{6}=\dfrac23$, positive because the angle is acute. Check: $\arctan5-\arctan1=78.69^\circ-45^\circ=33.69^\circ$ and $\tan33.69^\circ=0.667$. The negative options cannot be the tangent of an acute angle. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The values of $y$ for various values of $x$ are given in the table below.

| $x$ | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $y$ | 2 | 3.2 | 4.2 | 5 | 5.7 | 6.3 |

Using the trapezium rule, $\displaystyle\int_1^6 y\,dx\approx$
questions.corrige_markdown: There are $6$ ordinates, hence $5$ strips of width $h=1$. Trapezium rule: $\int_1^6y\,dx\approx\dfrac h2\big[y_1+y_6+2(y_2+y_3+y_4+y_5)\big]=\dfrac12\big[2+6.3+2(3.2+4.2+5+5.7)\big]=\dfrac12\big[8.3+2(18.1)\big]=\dfrac12(44.5)=22.25$. Option C, $22.52$, is a transposition of the digits. The sum of the six $y$ values alone is $26.4$ (option B), which is not the trapezium rule. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The number of arrangements of the letters of the word SUCCEEDED is
questions.corrige_markdown: SUCCEEDED has $9$ letters: S, U, C, C, E, E, D, E, D. The repeated letters are C (twice), E (three times) and D (twice); S and U occur once. The number of distinct arrangements is $\dfrac{9!}{2!\,2!\,3!}=\dfrac{362880}{24}=15120$. Option A forgets one of the two $2!$ factors; options C and D use $5!$, which would apply to only $5$ letters. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The equations of the vertical asymptotes to the graph of $f(x)=\dfrac{8}{x^2-4}$ are
questions.corrige_markdown:
Vertical asymptotes occur where the denominator is zero and the numerator is not: $x^2-4=(x-2)(x+2)=0$ gives $x=2$ and $x=-2$; the numerator $8$ is never zero, so $f(x)\to\pm\infty$ as $x\to\pm2$. The asymptotes are $x=-2$ and $x=2$. (There is also a horizontal asymptote $y=0$.)

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The solution set of the inequality $\dfrac{x+2}{x-1}\ge0$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The quotient is non-negative when numerator and denominator have the same sign, or when the numerator is $0$. Critical values: $x=-2$ (numerator zero, allowed because the inequality is $\ge$) and $x=1$ (denominator zero, never allowed). Sign table: for $x<-2$, $(x+2)<0$ and $(x-1)<0$, so the quotient is $>0$; for $-2<x<1$ the quotient is $<0$; for $x>1$ it is $>0$. So the solution is $x\le-2$ or $x>1$. Option C wrongly includes $x=1$, where the expression is undefined. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A committee of $5$, with at least one boy and at least one girl, is to be formed from $3$ boys and $5$ girls. The number of ways this committee can be formed if there are to be more girls than boys is
questions.corrige_markdown: With $5$ members, more girls than boys and at least one boy means $1$ boy and $4$ girls, or $2$ boys and $3$ girls ($3$ boys and $2$ girls has fewer girls than boys, and $0$ boys is excluded). $1$ boy, $4$ girls: $\binom31\binom54=3\times5=15$. $2$ boys, $3$ girls: $\binom32\binom53=3\times10=30$. Total $15+30=45$. Options B ($15$) and C ($30$) are each only one of the two cases. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The value of $a$ for which the quadratic equation $ax^2-10x+4=0$ has equal roots is
questions.corrige_markdown: Equal roots require the discriminant $b^2-4ac=0$: $(-10)^2-4(a)(4)=100-16a=0$, so $a=\dfrac{100}{16}=\dfrac{25}{4}$. Check: $\dfrac{25}4x^2-10x+4=0\iff25x^2-40x+16=0\iff(5x-4)^2=0$, giving the double root $x=\dfrac45$. Option B is the reciprocal. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A linear reduction of the relationship $y=ax^{n-1}$ produced the result $\log y=4\log x+2$. The values of the constants $\log a$ and $n$ are
questions.corrige_markdown: Take logarithms of $y=ax^{n-1}$: $\log y=\log a+(n-1)\log x$. Comparing with $\log y=4\log x+2$, the gradient gives $n-1=4$, so $n=5$ (option D forgets the $-1$ in the exponent and gives $4$), and the intercept gives $\log a=2$ (so $a=100$ if the logarithm is to base $10$). Option C takes $n-1=2$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The cardinality of the set $X=\{a,b,c\}$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The cardinality $n(X)$ of a finite set is the number of its elements. $X=\{a,b,c\}$ has $3$ elements, so $n(X)=3$. Option B, $8=2^3$, is the number of subsets of $X$ (the power set), not its cardinality. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The Cartesian equation of the curve with parametric equations $x=1-t^2$ and $y=4t$, where $t$ is a parameter is
questions.corrige_markdown: Eliminate $t$: from $y=4t$, $t=\dfrac y4$. Then $x=1-t^2=1-\dfrac{y^2}{16}$, so $16x=16-y^2$ (a parabola opening to the left with vertex $(1,0)$). Check with $t=1$: $(x,y)=(0,4)$ and $16(0)=16-16=0$. Options A and B come from squaring $\dfrac y4$ as $\dfrac{y^2}{4}$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
**SECTION B: STATISTICS**

Given that $P(A/B)=\dfrac{7}{10}$ and $P(A\cap B)=\dfrac1{10}$, $P(B)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: $P(A/B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$, so $P(B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(A/B)}=\dfrac{1/10}{7/10}=\dfrac17$. Option D, $\dfrac7{100}$, is the product $P(A/B)\times P(A\cap B)$, a misuse of the formula. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A discrete random variable $X$ takes values $1$, $2$ and $3$ with probabilities $0.2$, $0.3$ and $0.5$ respectively. The mean of $X$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: $E(X)=\sum xP(X=x)=1(0.2)+2(0.3)+3(0.5)=0.2+0.6+1.5=2.3$. (The probabilities sum to $1$, so the distribution is valid.) Option C, $1.0$, is $\sum P(X=x)$ and option A, $0.03$, is the product $0.2\times0.3\times0.5$: neither is a mean. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If a random variable $X$ is such that $Var(X)=4$, then $Var(3X-2)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: $Var(aX+b)=a^2Var(X)$: the constant $b$ does not change the spread, and the multiplier is squared. So $Var(3X-2)=3^2\times4=36$. Option A, $34=36-2$, wrongly applies the translation $-2$ to the variance. Option C, $12$, forgets to square the $3$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Given that the regression lines $y$ on $x$ and $x$ on $y$ are $y=6x-5$ and $x=0.3y+1$ respectively, the product moment correlation coefficient between the variables $x$ and $y$ is

*Options as printed:* A) 1.8   B) -1.8   C) 1.34   D) -1.34
questions.corrige_markdown:
The regression coefficients are $b_{yx}=6$ (gradient of $y$ on $x$) and $b_{xy}=0.3$ (gradient of $x$ on $y$), and $r^2=b_{yx}\,b_{xy}=6\times0.3=1.8$. Both gradients are positive, so $r$ is positive: $r=+\sqrt{1.8}\approx1.34$, the printed option C. BUT a product moment correlation coefficient must satisfy $-1\le r\le1$, so $r^2=1.8>1$ is impossible: the two printed lines cannot be the regression lines of any real data set (the product of the two gradients of genuine regression lines never exceeds $1$). The question is therefore defective; option C is only the value the formula produces mechanically (option A is $r^2$, and B and D carry the wrong sign).

**Intended answer: C (1.34).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: A random variable $X$ follows a Poisson distribution with parameter $\lambda$. If $P(X=0)=3P(X=1)$ then the value of $\lambda$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: $P(X=0)=e^{-\lambda}$ and $P(X=1)=\lambda e^{-\lambda}$. The condition gives $e^{-\lambda}=3\lambda e^{-\lambda}$; dividing by $e^{-\lambda}>0$, $1=3\lambda$, so $\lambda=\dfrac13$. Option A is the inverse, from reading the condition as $P(X=1)=3P(X=0)$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: To start a board game, a die is rolled repeatedly until a $6$ is obtained. The random variable ``the number of rolls made until a $6$ is obtained'' can best be modeled using
questions.corrige_markdown: The trials are independent, each has two outcomes (a $6$ with $p=\dfrac16$, or not), and we count the number of trials up to and including the FIRST success. That is the definition of a geometric distribution, $P(X=k)=\left(\dfrac56\right)^{k-1}\dfrac16$, $k=1,2,3,\dots$ A binomial distribution would count the number of $6$s in a FIXED number of rolls, a Poisson distribution counts events in an interval, and a uniform distribution would give all values the same probability. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If a random variable $X\sim Bin\left(12,\dfrac13\right)$, then $E(2X-3)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: For $X\sim Bin(n,p)$, $E(X)=np=12\times\dfrac13=4$. By linearity, $E(2X-3)=2E(X)-3=2(4)-3=5$. Option B, $8$, forgets the $-3$ and option C, $11$, adds it instead of subtracting. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $X$ is a continuous random variable with probability density function $f$, defined by $f(x)=\begin{cases}6x-6x^2,&0\le x\le1\\0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$ The mode of $X$ is
questions.corrige_markdown: The mode is the value of $x$ that maximises the density. $f'(x)=6-12x=0$ gives $x=\dfrac12$, and $f''(x)=-12<0$ so it is a maximum, with $f\left(\dfrac12\right)=3-\dfrac32=1.5$. At the end points $f(0)=f(1)=0$, so options B and C (the end points) give the smallest density, not the largest. (The density is valid: $\int_0^1(6x-6x^2)\,dx=3-2=1$.) **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If events $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive with $P(A)=\dfrac{2}{10}$ and $P(B)=\dfrac12$ then $P(A'\cap B')=$
questions.corrige_markdown: By De Morgan's law, $A'\cap B'=(A\cup B)'$, so $P(A'\cap B')=1-P(A\cup B)$. For mutually exclusive events $P(A\cap B)=0$, so $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)=\dfrac2{10}+\dfrac5{10}=\dfrac7{10}$. Hence $P(A'\cap B')=1-\dfrac7{10}=\dfrac3{10}$. Option C is $P(A\cup B)$ itself. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A set of bivariate data has the following summary statistics.

$n=10,\ \sum x=16,\ \sum y=38,\ \sum xy=119$

The covariance of $X$ and $Y$ for this data is
questions.corrige_markdown: The covariance is $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=\dfrac{\sum xy}{n}-\bar x\,\bar y=\dfrac{119}{10}-\dfrac{16}{10}\cdot\dfrac{38}{10}=11.9-6.08=5.82$. Option D, $58.2$, is the sum of products of deviations $S_{xy}=\sum xy-\dfrac{\sum x\sum y}{n}=119-60.8$, which is $n$ times the covariance. Option A comes from adding instead of subtracting $\bar x\bar y$ ($11.9+6.08=17.98$). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function $f$ defined by $f(x)=3e^{-3x},\ x>0$. The expectation of this exponential probability distribution is
questions.corrige_markdown: This is an exponential distribution with rate $\lambda=3$, so $E(X)=\dfrac1\lambda=\dfrac13$. Direct check: $E(X)=\int_0^\infty x\cdot3e^{-3x}\,dx=\left[-xe^{-3x}\right]_0^\infty+\int_0^\infty e^{-3x}\,dx=0+\dfrac13=\dfrac13$. Option A is the rate $\lambda$ itself, not the mean. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $A$ and $B$ are two independent events with $P(A)=\dfrac34$ and $P(B)=\dfrac13$, then $P(A\cap B')=$
questions.corrige_markdown: If $A$ and $B$ are independent then $A$ and $B'$ are also independent, so $P(A\cap B')=P(A)P(B')=\dfrac34\left(1-\dfrac13\right)=\dfrac34\cdot\dfrac23=\dfrac12$. Option C, $\dfrac1{12}$, is $P(A')\,P(B)$; option B is $P(A')$ and D is $P(B)$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The rankings assigned by two judges to $5$ contestants were such that $\sum d^2=4$. The Spearman's rank correlation coefficient for these rankings is
questions.corrige_markdown: With $n=5$ and $\sum d^2=4$: $r_s=1-\dfrac{6\sum d^2}{n(n^2-1)}=1-\dfrac{6\times4}{5\times24}=1-\dfrac{24}{120}=1-\dfrac15=\dfrac45$. Option C, $\dfrac15$, is the subtracted term only (the leading ``$1-$'' is forgotten). **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A random variable $X$ follows a normal distribution with mean $28$ and variance $4$. $P(25<X<34)=$
questions.corrige_markdown: $X\sim N(28,4)$, so $\sigma=2$ and $Z=\dfrac{X-28}{2}$. The limits become $z_1=\dfrac{25-28}{2}=-1.5$ and $z_2=\dfrac{34-28}{2}=3$. $P(25<X<34)=\phi(3)-\phi(-1.5)$, and by symmetry $\phi(-1.5)=1-\phi(1.5)$, so the probability is $\phi(3)-1+\phi(1.5)=\phi(3)+\phi(1.5)-1\approx0.99865+0.93319-1=0.9318$. Option A forgets that the lower limit is negative. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A year ago $54\%$ of the customers of a certain restaurant rated the services as excellent. Some weeks later, the proprietor employed a more experienced management with the belief that the customers' rating will step up. After some time, he decides to carry out a hypothesis test to cross check his belief. The null and alternative hypothesis he should use for this test are
questions.corrige_markdown: The null hypothesis states the old proportion, $H_0:p=0.54$. The proprietor believes the proportion of excellent ratings has INCREASED, which is a directional (one-tailed, upper-tail) alternative: $H_1:p>0.54$. Option A is the lower-tail test (a decrease), D is the two-tailed test (a change in either direction, with no belief about direction), and C is not a valid alternative since $H_1$ cannot be the same statement as $H_0$. **Answer: B.**
